lessons.title: What a Model Is: A Rule Learned From Data
lessons.description: A model is a rule that turns what you know into a guess about what you do not, and you can only call it good if it beats the simplest guess.
lessons.theory_md:
## Why this matters
Machine learning sounds like magic, so people trust it too easily or fear it. It is neither. A model is a rule that takes facts you have and gives a guess about something you do not. Once you see it that way, you can judge any model, from a spreadsheet formula to a large AI system, by the same question: is it better than a simple guess?

## The first principle
**A model is a rule for guessing, and it earns its place only by beating the simplest rule.**

The simplest rule is the **baseline**: always guess the average. If a clever model cannot beat "always guess the average", it has learned nothing useful, however advanced it sounds.

To compare, we need an error: how far each guess is from the truth. The **mean absolute error (MAE)** is the average distance between guess and truth, ignoring direction.

## A worked example
Mwangi Trading sells 40 products. We want to guess each product's selling price.

- **Baseline:** guess the average price, KES 1,359.17 for every product. The average miss is KES 1,027.09. That is a big miss, because a bag of nails and a ream of paper do not cost the same.
- **A rule:** guess the price from the cost: `price = cost x 1.25`. The average miss falls to KES 74.04.

The rule is about 14 times better than the baseline. It earned its place. The rule is also something you can read and explain, which matters later.

## Try it
SQL can do all of this. `AVG(unit_price)` gives the baseline. `ABS(a - b)` is the distance between two numbers. Averaging those distances gives the MAE. Use `unit_price` and `unit_cost` in `shop_products`.

## What you can and cannot claim
You can claim a rule is better than the baseline on these 40 products. You cannot yet claim it will work on new products, because we measured it on the same products we looked at. The next lesson fixes that.

## Say it in your own words
What is a model, what is the baseline, and why must a model beat the baseline?

## Do this in real life
Pick one number in your own work that you guess today, such as next month's sales or the time a job takes. Write the simplest guess (the average of the last few months) and how far off it usually is. That is your baseline.

lessons.title: Train and Test: Never Mark Your Own Homework
lessons.description: A model must be judged on data it has never seen, so we keep part of the data aside before we learn anything.
lessons.theory_md:
## Why this matters
A student who sees the exam questions in advance scores full marks and has learned nothing. A model judged on the data it learned from can look perfect and fail the first day in real life. The fix is simple and it is the most important habit in machine learning.

## The first principle
**Split the data first. Learn from one part, judge on the other.**

- **Training set:** the part the model learns from.
- **Test set:** the part kept aside, used only once to measure how good the model really is.

Anything you learn from, such as an average, must come from the training set only. If the test set leaks into the learning, the test no longer tells the truth. That mistake is called **leakage**.

## A worked example
We split the 40 products by number: odd product numbers are training, even are test. That gives 20 and 20, and it is the same split every time.

- The training average price is KES 1,103.65.
- The test average price is higher, KES 1,614.70. The two halves are not the same.

Guessing the training average for every test product misses by KES 1,178.03 on average. That is the honest baseline for this split. It is worse than the 1,027.09 we got before, because before we marked our own homework: the average was learned from the very products being scored.

## Try it
Use `product_id % 2 = 1` for training and `product_id % 2 = 0` for test. `%` gives the remainder after dividing, so an odd number leaves 1.

## What you can and cannot claim
A fixed split is fair and repeatable, but one split can be lucky or unlucky. Twenty test products is a small test. Treat the result as a first honest estimate, not a promise.

## Say it in your own words
Why do we split the data before learning, and what is leakage?

## Do this in real life
Take a list of results from your own work, such as monthly sales. Decide a rule from the older months only, then check it on the recent months you did not use. Write whether it held up.

lessons.title: Fit a Line by Hand
lessons.description: Linear regression finds the straight line that best predicts one number from another, and you can compute it with sums.
lessons.theory_md:
## Why this matters
Many useful models are just a straight line. If you can build one by hand, you will never treat a library call as magic, and you will notice when it is wrong.

## The first principle
**The best line is the one that makes the squared misses smallest, and it comes from five sums.**

For a line `price = intercept + slope x cost`, take the training rows and compute:

- `n`, the number of rows
- `sum_x`, the sum of the costs
- `sum_y`, the sum of the prices
- `sum_xx`, the sum of each cost times itself
- `sum_xy`, the sum of each cost times its price

Then:

`slope = (n x sum_xy - sum_x x sum_y) / (n x sum_xx - sum_x x sum_x)`

`intercept = (sum_y - slope x sum_x) / n`

## A worked example
On the 20 training products:

- n = 20, sum_x = 17,610, sum_y = 22,073, sum_xx = 26,064,850, sum_xy = 32,486,805.
- slope = 1.236: each extra KES 1 of cost adds about KES 1.24 to the price.
- intercept = 15.33.

So the model is `price = 15.33 + 1.236 x cost`. The slope matches what the shop does: it adds about a quarter on top of cost, plus a little extra.

## Try it
Work in steps. First get the five sums with one query. Then put them in a `WITH` block and compute the slope. Multiply by `1.0` or use decimals so the division is not rounded down to whole numbers, which is what SQL does when both sides are whole numbers.

## What you can and cannot claim
The line describes the relationship in the training products. It says nothing about why prices are set that way, and it may fail for products priced by a different rule, such as a promotion.

## Say it in your own words
What does the slope of a line tell you, and why do we compute it from the training data only?

## Do this in real life
Pick two numbers from your work that move together, such as advertising spend and sales. Write down roughly how much one rises when the other rises by one unit. That is a slope, even if you never computed it.

quiz.question: What does a slope of 1.236 mean in price = 15.33 + 1.236 x cost?
options: Each extra KES 1 of cost adds about KES 1.24 to the price
The cost is 1.236 times the price
quiz.explanation: The slope is the change in the guess for each one-unit change in the input.

quiz.question: Which data do we use to compute the sums?
quiz.explanation: Learning from the test set would be leakage.

quiz.question: What goes wrong if both sides of a division in SQL are whole numbers?
options: The result is rounded down to a whole number
quiz.explanation: SQLite divides whole numbers as whole numbers, so multiply by 1.0 first.

quiz.question: What does the intercept represent?
options: The guess when the input is zero
quiz.explanation: The intercept is where the line starts.

quiz.question: A line fits the training products very well. What can you NOT conclude?
options: The slope describes the training products
The shop prices at about cost plus a quarter
It explains why the shop chose those prices
It beats the baseline on the training set
quiz.explanation: A fitted line describes a pattern; it does not explain the reason for it.

lessons.title: Measure the Miss: MAE, MSE and the Worst Case
lessons.description: Different error measures answer different questions, so choose the one that matches what a miss costs you.
lessons.theory_md:
## Why this matters
"The model is 95 percent good" means nothing until you say what a miss costs. A small miss on a cheap item and a huge miss on one expensive item are not the same problem.

## The first principle
**Pick the error measure that matches the cost of being wrong.**

- **MAE** (mean absolute error): the average size of the miss. Easy to read: "off by KES 100 on average."
- **MSE** (mean squared error): the average of the squared miss. Squaring makes big misses count far more, so one terrible guess shows up.
- **The worst case**: the single biggest miss. It matters when one failure is expensive.

Always compare against the baseline, on the test set.

## A worked example
Our line is `price = 15.33 + 1.236 x cost`. On the 20 test products:

- MAE of the line: KES 103.79. The honest baseline MAE was 1,178.03.
- MSE of the baseline: about 2,897,496. MSE of the line: about 30,985. The line is about 94 times better by this measure, so the big baseline misses disappear.
- The worst single miss is Acaricide 1L, off by KES 548.29. The line suits most products, but not this one.

The worst case is a question to ask: why is this product different? It may have a special price rule, a typing mistake, or a real exception worth knowing.

## Try it
Squaring in SQL is `x * x`. Use the learned numbers from the last lesson inside the query: `15.33 + 1.236 * unit_cost`. Score only the test products (even `product_id`).

## What you can and cannot claim
A low average error does not mean no bad misses. Always look at the worst few cases before trusting a model.

## Say it in your own words
What is the difference between MAE and MSE, and why look at the worst miss?

## Do this in real life
Take any forecast you have made. Write the average miss, then the biggest miss, and say which one hurt you more.

quiz.explanation: If one miss can cost a fortune, the average hides the danger.

lessons.title: Classifying: Predicting a Category and Beating 'Always Paid'
lessons.description: When the answer is a category, accuracy is the share right, and the baseline is always guessing the most common category.
lessons.theory_md:
## Why this matters
Many real questions are yes or no: will this customer pay late, is this email spam, will this machine fail. Predicting a category is called **classification**. The danger is a number that sounds good and means nothing.

## The first principle
**Accuracy is the share of guesses that are right, and it must be compared with the baseline of always guessing the most common answer.**

If 72 out of 100 sales are paid on the spot, a model that says "paid" every time is already 72 percent accurate. A model that scores 70 percent is worse than doing nothing, even though 70 sounds high.

## A worked example
Mwangi Trading made 2,046 sales in 2025: 1,480 paid at once and 566 sold on credit.

- **Baseline:** always say "paid". Accuracy is 72.3 percent.
- **A simple rule:** if the sale total is above KES 20,000, predict credit, otherwise paid. Accuracy is 65.6 percent.

The rule is worse than the baseline. Big sales are not a good signal for who will not pay. The result is useful: it tells you not to build a credit warning on the sale total alone.

## Try it
A condition in SQL is true (1) or false (0), so `SUM(payment_status = 'paid')` counts the paid sales. Multiply by `100.0` and divide by `COUNT(*)` for a percentage. A rule's right guesses are sales where `total > 20000` and the status is `credit`, or `total <= 20000` and the status is `paid`.

## What you can and cannot claim
You can say the rule did not beat the baseline on these sales. You cannot say totals never help: a different split or a different signal might work, which is what the next lessons explore.

## Say it in your own words
What is the baseline for a yes or no question, and why can a model with high accuracy still be useless?

## Do this in real life
Think of a yes or no decision in your work, such as whether a customer will pay on time. Write how often the answer is yes. A rule must beat that number to be worth using.

quiz.question: What is the baseline for a classifier?
options: Always guessing the most common category
quiz.explanation: The simplest rule is to always pick the most common answer.

quiz.question: 72.3 percent of sales are paid at once. A model has 70 percent accuracy. Is it useful?
options: No, it is worse than always saying paid
quiz.explanation: It does worse than a rule that never thinks.

quiz.question: In SQL, what does SUM(payment_status = 'paid') count?
quiz.explanation: A true condition counts as 1, so the sum counts the rows where it is true.

quiz.question: The 'total above 20,000 means credit' rule scored 65.6 percent against 72.3 percent. What follows?
options: Sale total alone is not a good signal for credit risk
quiz.explanation: The rule failed on this data, which is a finding in itself.

quiz.question: Why multiply by 100.0 rather than 100 in the percentage?
options: So the division keeps decimals instead of rounding down to a whole number
quiz.explanation: Whole-number division in SQL drops the decimals.

lessons.title: Precision, Recall and the Confusion Matrix
lessons.description: Accuracy hides the mistakes that matter, so we count the four kinds of answer and ask two better questions.
lessons.theory_md:
## Why this matters
A model that warns about credit risk can fail in two ways: it can warn about a customer who would have paid (a false alarm), or it can stay silent about one who will not pay (a miss). The two failures cost different things, and one accuracy number hides both.

## The first principle
**Count the four outcomes, then ask: when it warns, how often is it right (precision), and of all the real cases, how many did it catch (recall)?**

The **confusion matrix** has four counts. Here a "positive" is a credit sale:

- **True positive (tp):** warned, and it was credit.
- **False positive (fp):** warned, but it was paid.
- **False negative (fn):** stayed silent, but it was credit.
- **True negative (tn):** stayed silent, and it was paid.

`precision = tp / (tp + fp)` and `recall = tp / (tp + fn)`.

## A worked example
With the rule "total above 20,000 means credit":

- tp = 236, fp = 374, fn = 330, tn = 1,106.
- Precision = 236 / 610 = 38.7 percent. Of the sales it warned about, fewer than 4 in 10 were credit.
- Recall = 236 / 566 = 41.7 percent. It caught fewer than half of the credit sales.

Raise the threshold to 40,000 and precision stays about the same (38.4 percent) while recall collapses to 5.8 percent. The warning gets rarer without getting more accurate. That tells you the total is a weak signal.

## Try it
Count each case with `SUM(condition)`. The positives the rule warns about are `total > 20000`. Divide counts with `100.0 *` to keep decimals.

## What you can and cannot claim
Which of precision and recall matters more depends on cost: a missed fraud is worse than a false alarm for a bank, while too many false alarms makes staff ignore the system. The model cannot choose that for you.

## Say it in your own words
What are precision and recall, and why is accuracy alone not enough?

## Do this in real life
Think of an alert you get at work or home. Count how often it fires when nothing is wrong, and how often something goes wrong without it firing. That is precision and recall in daily life.

quiz.explanation: Recall is the share of real cases caught.

options: The warning got rarer without getting more accurate
quiz.explanation: A stricter rule that is not more accurate just misses more.

options: When a missed case is much more costly than a false alarm
quiz.explanation: If missing a real case is expensive, false alarms are the price.

lessons.title: Overfitting: Memorising Is Not Learning
lessons.description: A model that copies its training data looks perfect there and fails on anything new.
lessons.theory_md:
## Why this matters
A student who memorises last year's exam gets full marks on last year's paper and fails this year's. Models do the same. The more freedom a model has, the easier it is for it to memorise the noise in its training data and call that learning.

## The first principle
**A model that is much better on the data it learned from than on new data has memorised, not learned.**

The gap between the training score and the test score is the warning. A simple rule usually has a small gap. A model that memorises has a very large one.

An easy memoriser is the **nearest neighbour** rule: to guess a new sale's status, find the training sale with the closest total and copy its status.

## A worked example
We take the first 400 sales: odd sale numbers train, even sale numbers test.

- On its own training sales, the nearest-neighbour rule scores 98.5 percent. Each sale finds itself, so it is nearly always right. It looks brilliant.
- On the unseen test sales it scores 65.0 percent.
- The simple threshold rule (total above 20,000 means credit) scores 67.0 percent on the same test sales.
- Always guessing "paid" scores 72.5 percent.

The memoriser has a gap of more than 30 points, and on new data it is worse than guessing "paid". Its training score was a lie.

## Try it
Use `sale_id <= 400` to keep the first 400 sales and `sale_id % 2` to split. Pair every test sale with every training sale, then number each test sale's pairs from the closest with `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY q.sale_id ORDER BY ABS(tr.total - q.total), tr.sale_id)` and keep number 1. The second sort key, `sale_id`, settles ties the same way each time.

## What you can and cannot claim
A gap between training and test is evidence of memorising; a small gap does not prove the model is good, only that it is not memorising. You still compare with the baseline.

## Say it in your own words
What is overfitting, and how do you spot it?

## Do this in real life
Think of a habit that works only in one place, such as a trick that works with one supplier. Write down why it might fail with another. That is overfitting in daily life.

quiz.explanation: Overfitting is memorising noise instead of learning a pattern.

quiz.question: How do you spot it?

quiz.explanation: A big gap shows it has not generalised.

quiz.explanation: Each training sale finds itself, so its training score means nothing.

options: The memoriser is worse than guessing
quiz.explanation: A model below the baseline has added nothing.

quiz.question: Why add sale_id as a second sort key when picking the nearest sale?
options: So ties are settled the same way every time
To change the result on purpose
quiz.explanation: Without it, equal distances could return different rows.

lessons.title: Nearest Neighbours: Predict From Similar Cases
lessons.description: To predict something new, find the most similar cases you already know and average what happened to them.
lessons.theory_md:
## Why this matters
People predict by comparison all the time: "this house is like the one next door, so it should sell for about the same." The nearest-neighbours method does exactly that, and it needs no formula. It also shows how a model can be understood by looking at the cases behind each guess.

## The first principle
**Similar inputs tend to have similar outputs, so predict from the k closest known cases.**

You choose:

- how to measure **distance** (here, the difference in cost), and
- **k**, how many neighbours to use. A small k follows every wiggle; a large k smooths them out.

Always look for neighbours in the training set only.

## A worked example
We want to predict the price of product 10, Nails 2kg, with cost KES 975. Its three nearest training neighbours by cost are:

- Paint 4L, cost distance 5, price 1,245.
- A4 paper ream, cost distance 150, price 1,089.
- Cement 50kg, cost distance 235, price 1,006.

The prediction is the average of the three prices: KES 1,113.33. The real price is 1,316. The miss is KES 202.67. The line from lesson 3 would have guessed 1,220.43 for this product, a miss of 95.57. A neighbours method is simple and honest, but not always the best.

## Try it
Distance is `ABS(unit_cost - (SELECT unit_cost FROM shop_products WHERE product_id = 10))`. Keep only training products (`product_id % 2 = 1`), order by distance then by `product_id`, and `LIMIT 3`. Then average their prices.

## What you can and cannot claim
The result depends on k, on how distance is measured and on which cases are in the training set. It cannot go beyond the cases it has seen: a product far from all the others gets a poor guess.

## Say it in your own words
How does nearest neighbours predict, and what do the choices of distance and k change?

## Do this in real life
Think of a new job you are asked to quote. Find the three most similar jobs you have done and average what they cost. You have just used nearest neighbours.

quiz.explanation: More neighbours means a smoother, less noisy guess.

quiz.explanation: A case that finds itself makes the score meaningless.

Which product would nearest neighbours predict worst?

quiz.explanation: With no close cases, there is nothing similar to learn from.

lessons.title: Features: What the Model Is Allowed to Know
lessons.description: A model is only as good as the facts it is given, and some facts are only known after the answer, which makes them cheating.
lessons.theory_md:
## Why this matters
Most of the skill in practical machine learning is choosing what to feed the model, not which model to use. The facts you give it are called **features**. A good feature carries real signal. A bad one adds noise. The worst is a feature that secretly contains the answer.

## The first principle
**A feature is only allowed if you would know it at the moment you need the prediction.**

Using something you only learn afterwards is **leakage**, and it makes a model look brilliant in testing and useless in real life.

## A worked example
We want to warn about credit sales before they are made. Look at what each feature tells us:

- **Sale total:** weak, as the last lessons showed.
- **Customer segment:** strong. Retail customers bought on credit in 3.9 percent of their sales, Institutions in 39.1 percent and Wholesale in 40.1 percent.
- **Has the customer made a payment on this sale?** This looks powerful: every paid sale has a payment, and 137 credit sales have none. But you only know about payments after the sale. It is leakage, and a warning built on it would arrive too late.

Using the segment, we can ignore Retail customers (33.6 percent of sales) and watch the rest: that means watching 66.4 percent of sales while catching 95.2 percent of the credit sales. The feature does not make a perfect yes or no rule, but it tells you where to look.

## Try it
Join `shop_sales` to `shop_customers` on `customer_id` to reach `segment`. For the leakage check use `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM shop_payments p WHERE p.sale_id = s.sale_id)` to find sales with no payment row.

## What you can and cannot claim
A strong feature does not prove cause. Wholesale customers may buy on credit because of the terms the shop gave them, not because of who they are. Say "is linked to", not "causes".

## Say it in your own words
What is a feature, and what makes a feature leakage?

## Do this in real life
Think of a prediction you make at work. List what you know at the time you decide, and what you only learn later. Only the first list may be used.

options: The feature points you where to look
quiz.explanation: It narrows the search at a small cost.

quiz.question: Why say 'is linked to' rather than 'causes'?
options: A pattern in data does not show why it happens
quiz.explanation: A link can be due to terms, history or something else.

lessons.title: Language Models: What They Do, What They Cost and Where They Fail
lessons.description: A language model predicts the next piece of text, so you can estimate its size and cost with arithmetic, and plan for its mistakes.
lessons.theory_md:
## Why this matters
Large language models (LLMs) now write, summarise and answer questions. People use them without knowing what they are doing or what they cost. A founder or analyst who can reason about them avoids two traps: believing every answer and being surprised by the bill.

## The first principle
**An LLM predicts the next piece of text from the text so far. It is built to sound right, not to be right.**

Three working facts follow:

- **Tokens:** models read and write in small pieces of text called tokens. A rough rule for English is about 4 characters per token. Providers charge by tokens, in and out.
- **Context window:** the model can only consider a limited amount of text per request. Anything beyond it is not seen.
- **Hallucination:** it can state false things confidently, because fluency is not truth. Anything that matters must be checked against a source.

## A worked example
We want an assistant to answer questions about our 40 products by sending the product names with each question.

- The 40 names total 526 characters, about 132 tokens by the 4-characters rule.
- Add 50 tokens for the question and instructions: 182 tokens per call.
- Suppose, as an example only, a provider charged 0.5 currency units per 1,000 tokens. One call costs 182 x 0.5 / 1,000 = 0.091.
- At 300 questions a month that is 27.30, and the text easily fits a window of 8,000 tokens.

The rate here is invented for practice. Real prices and window sizes differ by provider and change often, so read your provider's current page before you plan.

## Try it
`LENGTH(name)` gives the characters in a name, and `SUM(LENGTH(name)) / 4.0` estimates tokens (use `4.0` so SQL keeps decimals). Multiply by the number of calls and the rate.

## What you can and cannot claim
The 4-characters rule is an estimate, and it is worse for other languages and for code. A model's answer can look right and be wrong. You can claim a cost estimate and a size check. You cannot claim the answers are correct without checking them.

## Say it in your own words
What is a token, and why can an LLM be confident and wrong?

## Do this in real life
Pick one question you often answer for customers. Write down what text the model would need, estimate its tokens, and say how you would check each answer.

lessons.title: Retrieval: Giving a Model the Right Facts
lessons.description: Instead of trusting a model's memory, find the relevant documents first, show them to it, and measure how well the search works.
lessons.theory_md:
## Why this matters
A language model does not know your business, and its memory can be wrong. The common fix is **retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)**: first search your own documents for the passages that matter, then give those passages to the model and ask it to answer from them. The answer is only as good as the search.

## The first principle
**Measure the search before you trust the answer.**

- **Retrieval:** score each document against the question and keep the top k.
- **Evaluation set:** a small list of questions with the documents that are truly relevant, written by a person.
- **Recall at k:** of the truly relevant documents, how many are in the top k?

If retrieval fails, the model never sees the right facts, and it will fill the gap with a guess.

## A worked example
Our documents are the six findings in `shop_actions`. The question is "Which problems involve a late or expensive supplier?" We score each document with three keyword checks: the finding contains "late", the finding contains "price", the action contains "supplier".

- Action 2 (Highland Agrovet delivers about a week late) scores 2.
- Action 3 (Rift Valley Hardware raised its prices) scores 1.
- The other four score 0.

A person labelled actions 2 and 3 as the relevant ones. The top 2 by score are exactly 2 and 3, so recall at 2 is 100 percent.

A keyword score is crude. It would miss a document that says "delayed" instead of "late". Real systems often compare meaning rather than words, but the evaluation habit is the same.

## Try it
A condition like `finding LIKE '%late%'` is 1 or 0, so you can add conditions together to make a score. Order by score descending, with `action_id` as the tie-breaker. A relevant list can be written in the query with `VALUES (2), (3)`.

## What you can and cannot claim
A good score on six documents and one question proves little. You can claim the search works for this question. A real evaluation set needs many questions, and it should be written before you tune the search.

## Say it in your own words
What is retrieval, and how do you know the search is working?

## Do this in real life
Choose five questions your customers or team ask often. For each, write which document or note holds the answer. That list is your first evaluation set.

quiz.question: What problem does retrieval solve?
options: It gives the model relevant facts instead of relying on its memory
quiz.explanation: Retrieval supplies the facts the model should answer from.

quiz.question: What is an evaluation set?
options: Questions paired with the documents a person says are relevant
quiz.explanation: It is the answer key for the search.

quiz.question: Recall at 2 is 100 percent. What does it mean?
options: Both relevant documents are in the top 2
The search is perfect for all questions
quiz.explanation: All relevant documents were retrieved in the top k for this question.

quiz.question: Why can a keyword score miss a good document?
options: A document may say 'delayed' where you searched for 'late'
quiz.explanation: Keywords match words, not meaning.

quiz.question: When should you write the evaluation set?
options: After tuning the search, to match it
Before tuning, so the test is honest
quiz.explanation: Writing it after tuning would repeat the leakage mistake.

lessons.title: Keeping a Model Honest After Launch
lessons.description: A model that worked yesterday can quietly stop working, so you watch the data it sees and decide in advance what triggers a check.
lessons.theory_md:
## Why this matters
Building a model is the start, not the end. The world changes: customers change, prices change, a supplier changes. A model trained on last year's behaviour can drift into being wrong without any error message. Operating a model, often called **MLOps**, is mostly about noticing that early and cheaply.

## The first principle
**Decide in advance what you will watch, what counts as a problem, and what you will do about it.**

You watch three kinds of thing:

- **The data it sees:** has the mix of customers, sizes or categories changed? This is **drift**.
- **The results it gives:** has accuracy or error moved?
- **The practical costs:** how much it costs per call and how long it takes.

You also keep **versions**: which model, which data and which settings produced each answer, so a surprising result can be traced.

## A worked example
We watch the credit share of sales by quarter in 2025:

- Quarter 1: 26.7 percent. Quarter 2: 30.9. Quarter 3: 28.5. Quarter 4: 24.9.
- The first half averaged 28.8 percent, which we take as the normal level when the model was set up.
- We set a rule: check if a quarter is more than 3 points away from normal.

Quarters 1 to 3 are within the rule. Quarter 4 is 3.9 points below, so it is flagged for a check. A flag is not an error. It says "look here": maybe a stricter credit policy was introduced, maybe the customer mix changed. A person looks at the cause before retraining anything.

## Try it
Quarter number from a date: `(CAST(strftime('%m', sale_date) AS INTEGER) + 2) / 3`. The normal level is the credit share of quarters 1 and 2 together. Compare each quarter with it using `ABS(...) > 3`.

## What you can and cannot claim
A drift flag shows that something changed, not that the model is wrong. A quiet dashboard does not prove the model is right: you need real outcomes to check accuracy. Choose the threshold before you look, or you will fit it to what you see.

## Say it in your own words
What is drift, and what should you decide before a model goes live?

## Do this in real life
Pick one number you check at work every month. Write the normal range, what size of change makes you look closer, and who you tell. That is a monitoring plan.

quiz.question: What is drift?
options: A change in the data or behaviour the model sees compared with when it was set up
quiz.explanation: Drift means the world has moved from what the model was built on.

quiz.question: Quarter 4 credit share is 3.9 points below normal and the rule flags changes over 3 points. What does a flag mean?
options: A person should look for the cause
quiz.explanation: A flag says look here; it does not diagnose.

quiz.question: Why keep versions of the model, data and settings?
options: To trace a surprising result back to what produced it
quiz.explanation: Without versions you cannot explain a change.

quiz.question: When should you choose the alert threshold?
options: After seeing the results, to fit them
Before looking, so it is not tuned to what you see
quiz.explanation: Choosing it afterwards repeats the leakage mistake.

quiz.question: The dashboard shows no drift. What can you conclude?
options: The inputs look like before; accuracy still needs real outcomes to check
quiz.explanation: No drift in the inputs says nothing about whether the guesses are right.
